title: ‘April X’ Review: Connor Storrie Bides His Time in a Generic Sci-Fi Clone
description: It would be nice to say that Connor Storrie burns up the screen in “April X,” the star’s first film vehicle released since TV’s “Heated Rivalry” mad
body:
It would be nice to say that Connor Storrie burns up the screen in “April X,” the star’s first film vehicle released since TV’s “Heated Rivalry” made him hot property, but it would be overstating the case. Appropriating Harrison Ford’s “Blade Runner” frown, among a few other things nicked from that sci-fi classic in this sci-fi filler, Storrie capably shoulders a grim, po-faced tale of human cloning and trafficking in a greige dystopian future, but there’s not much for him to work with here — and he mostly projects the aura of a working actor dutifully waiting for something better to come along. Which it did, so job done. But you can hardly blame “April X” for riding his sudden celebrity, securing a theatrical release and escaping the straight-to-VOD morass that would appear to be its natural habitat.
	

	Surely only Storrie’s most ardently committed new fans will venture out to see this, though: It’s hardly an embarrassing blot on his résumé, but it’ll be forgotten long before the second-season premiere of the queer hockey phenomenon. For writer-director Michel K. Parandi, making his feature-length debut, “April X” will be a more critical calling card — and duly shows off some resourceful technical ability on a cramped budget. But his script, co-written with regular collaborator Jack Coulter, is less impressive, welding together story scraps from other, better films to rather turbid, uninvolving effect. It occupies a similar genre space to the recent release “Hot Spot,” Agnieszka Smoczynska’s comparably scrappy, patched-together vision of compromised human identity in the middle-distance future; that film was a misfire, but a measure of its imaginative eccentricity would still be welcome here.
	

	The year is unspecified, but the fatigued brutalist housing blocks of outer Bucharest are still standing: Though it doesn’t specify a location either, “April X” uses the present-day wear and tear of the Romanian capital, where the film was shot on location, as shorthand for a world collapsing into concrete ruin. The odd hi-tech drone adds some futuristic pizzazz to the film’s exterior vistas, but the new technologies defining the narrative aren’t of the gleaming, brave-new-world variety: People are being cloned in grubby, shadowed fashion, while memories and dreams can be captured and downloaded onto surprisingly retro-looking data devices.

	In this grimy waking nightmare, twins Baxter (Storrie) and April (German actor Lilly Krug) barely eke out a living doing a variety of sketchy jobs, some more criminal than others. He traffics organs on the black market, while she has a special gift for dreaming: At a time, apparently, when nobody has slumber visions anymore, hers are enviably lucid and vivid, to a marketable degree. April’s selling of her dreams to others wishing to experience her sensations isn’t a fresh idea — paging “Strange Days” — but it’s one of the more fertile ones here, and goes frustratingly unexploited as the film continues to probe a single glum reality. 

	We’re more concerned with Baxter, whose underworld dealings eventually see him run afoul of local gangster Klein (Serban Pavlu), and the twins’ combined savings aren’t enough to allay the severe consequences. Soon April disappears, and Baxter’s desperate search for her begins. It’s ongoing when the story suddenly lurches five years into the future: The world looks much the same, but his hair is briefly longer, while April has seemingly been cloned into a number of identikit sex workers. Whether her brother can locate her soul in any one of them, or somehow implant it via her recorded memories, is the film’s big existential question — but the characters themselves aren’t drawn with enough warmth or personality for us to really care either way.

	Storrie soldiers through it all with a clenched jaw and a steely gaze, but the film’s world never comes fully to life. Nathan Haugaard’s sheeny widescreen lensing and Oana Novicov’s distressed production design ensure it looks pretty good, but “April X” is missing the granular particulars and textures that might make us believe it: The narrative, likewise, is just cohesive enough, but the details of Baxter’s life and livelihood are so muddy that he doesn’t have our full attention. Parandi’s film winds up outlining a dystopia more dull than devastating — though perhaps that’s the future we should really be fearing.

schema.headline: ‘April X’ Review: Connor Storrie Bides His Time in a Generic Sci-Fi Clone

title: New York’s Inaugural Muslim Film Festival Aims to Move Past Counter-Narratives, Unveils Lineup, Jury (EXCLUSIVE)
description: A festival launching Oct. 11 at Manhattan’s SVA Theatre is positioning itself as an answer to the flattened, stereotyped picture of Muslims Western
body:
A festival launching Oct. 11 at Manhattan’s SVA Theatre is positioning itself as an answer to the flattened, stereotyped picture of Muslims Western media often traffics in. The New York Muslim Film Festival (NYMFF), billed as the city’s first for Muslim filmmakers, wants them telling their own stories.

	Hassan Babar, the festival’s artistic director, said such stories should not merely serve as counter-narratives. “They should be the establishing paradigm,” Babar said.
	

	The one-day event will screen 12 shorts from seven countries, with documentaries, dramas, comedies, animation and experimental pieces in the mix. Women make up a majority of the program’s directors.


	“This festival exists because those stories deserve a stage in this city, not on the margins of someone else’s,” said Nawal Mubin, the festival’s co-founder and director.

	The day will open with a reception for filmmakers and industry guests. Two blocks of six films each, running roughly an hour apiece, will precede the awards and the jury announcement.

	Emmy winner Aasif Mandvi, a longtime “The Daily Show” correspondent who also starred in Paramount+ series “Evil,” sits on the six-member jury. He is joined by Arab-American writer-director Darine Hotait, founder of Cinephilia Productions, whose shorts have aired on HBO, AMC, SundanceTV and the BBC; Munir Atalla, head of production and acquisitions at Watermelon Pictures and a former Netflix creative executive; and producer Abubakar Khan, whose resume includes “The Glassworker,” Pakistan’s entry for the 2024 Oscars, and SXSW 2023 audience award winner “Mustache.”
	

	Rounding out the panel are Lebanese-American filmmaker Sarah Mokh, a Sundance Feature Film Fellow who recently wrapped her first feature, “The Alchemy of Being Okay,” which Khan is producing, and Egyptian-American actor Abubakr Ali. Ali has roles coming up in Bassam Tariq’s “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother,” opposite Mahershala Ali, and Sean Durkin’s A24 film “Deep Cuts,” and recently appeared in Kathryn Bigelow’s “A House of Dynamite.”

	Streamer Watermelon+ is behind the festival’s Watermelon+ Discovery Award. Its winner, whether filmmaker or rights holder, will give the platform an exclusive license to show the film for a limited period. The Islamic Scholarship Fund, New York production and post house Lost in Space, and Aneesa Talks, which filmmaker Aneesa Khan founded to support South Asian and Muslim creatives, have also signed on as partners.

	The program ranges widely in tone and subject. Justin Mashouf’s documentary “$17.74” follows a former gang member, behind bars since the 1980s, whose gesture of support for Gaza from inside prison set off a viral wave of solidarity. In Karim Emara’s Qatar-U.S. dramedy “Baba Is Melting,” a son phones his father, who is waiting in the car before Friday prayer in Doha, to challenge him over a hidden second marriage.

	Zaid Ahmed Hassan’s “Ghusl” centers on a son whose dying father asks him to learn Islamic burial rites, while Basma Khalifa’s U.K. experimental piece “Henna” follows the henna plant’s life cycle alongside women from 16 African and SWANA countries. Sima Naseem’s Canada-Pakistan animation “My Friend in the Jingle Truck” combines stop-motion and 2D to tell of a Karachi girl who meets a magical bird.

	In Alex Aljouni’s “Bukra,” a young Syrian refugee whose sweepstakes prize is a soccer ball rushes to collect it in time for one last match with her best friend before he is gone for good. One daring move reopens old rifts among three generations of Afghan women in Negine Jasmine Sekandari and Ayda Rojhantalab’s comedy “Haram Salami,” as they weigh who they are against what custom demands and what they want.

	Maram Taibah’s Saudi fantasy “Malika” explores a girl’s bond with her grandmother, and the pull between wildness and the obedience expected of girls, through a magical-realist world spun from a child’s imagination. In Bilal Shams Khan’s Pakistani drama “Sabr O Shukar,” 10-year-old Akram learns about patience and gratitude while chasing his dream of a bicycle.
	

	Imran J. Khan’s “The Boy With Dinosaur Head” pits a troubled boy who believes he is a dinosaur against a teacher set on pulling him back to reality, and their short encounter stays with both of them. Ilhan Abdullahi and Sherry Rashidan’s Canadian comedy “Unqualified” follows Warsan, the lone Muslim at her workplace, who is handed the job of spiritually cleansing a lunchroom said to be haunted and must clear out the spirits, armed with her faith and a string of misunderstandings, before she loses her job.

	Lyna Tadount and Sofian Chouaib’s French drama “Ya Hanouni” centers on two parents vying to be their baby’s first word, until their lighthearted contest is cut short by an event that upends their lives.

	Babar, a Toronto-based actor and producer, co-heads programming with Aneesa Khan, who also leads communications. Mubin, a New York director-producer, co-founded the festival with filmmaker and post-production specialist Giuseppe de Matteis. Both work at Lost in Space.

schema.headline: New York’s Inaugural Muslim Film Festival Aims to Move Past Counter-Narratives, Unveils Lineup, Jury (EXCLUSIVE)

title: George Cheeks May Be Poised for Expanded TV Role at Skydance Post Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger
description: Paramount TV media chair George Cheeks, whose domain has included all of CBS in addition to the Paramount cable networks, is said to be in line for
body:
Paramount TV media chair George Cheeks, whose domain has included all of CBS in addition to the Paramount cable networks, is said to be in line for an expanded oversight at the newly merged Paramount-Warner Bros. entity (which will be named “Skydance,” the company revealed Friday).

	Skydance would not comment, but Cheeks has been seen as a strong lieutenant overseeing the TV properties under Paramount ever since Skydance took control of the company last August. Prior to that, Cheeks was one of the three co-CEOs of Paramount Global — and was the only one of that triumvirate to make the transition to the new company.
	

	Speculation and rumors of how the structure on the TV network and studio side might play out have been heavy over the past few days, now that the question of how the streaming structure at the merged company has been settled (with HBO boss Casey Bloys on top and Paramount direct-to-consumer head Cindy Holland exiting).


	Many of the questions in the more traditional Hollywood world of TV networks and studios — still a hefty revenue driver — have centered on what roles Skydance head David Ellison might have in mind for Warner Bros. TV Group and WBD U.S. Networks chairman/CEO Channing Dungey and Cheeks. Both execs are well-liked and respected, and both boast tremendous domains, consisting of both studios and networks.

	One scenario making the rounds has Cheeks potentially overseeing all of the vast TV holdings of the combined company, but so far, there’s no firm confirmation and a final structure isn’t expected to be announced until next week.
	

	All eyes will also be on what role Ellison picks for Dungey, whose tenure at Warner Bros. TV Group continues to be extremely successful. Under Dungey, the studio produces more than 80 original series for more than 20 platforms, including HBO, HBO Max and others, with series like “Ted Lasso,” “Abbott Elementary”, “The Bachelor” franchise, “Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage,” “The Jennifer Hudson Show,” “The Pitt,” “Running Point,” “Shrinking,” “Rooster,” “The Voice” and the upcoming “Harry Potter” series. So far this year, the division has landed 13 new series orders and 13 series renewals, while “The Pitt” just landed six Emmys — including its second for outstanding drama.

	Dungey also took on oversight of WBD’s U.S. Networks in 2025, including Discovery Channel, Food Network, HGTV, Investigation Discovery, TLC, Adult Swim, Animal Planet, Cartoon Network, Cooking Channel, HLN, OWN, Science Channel, TBS, TNT, Travel Channel, Tru TV and Turner Classic Movies.

	When Variety spoke to Dungey last month, she said she had met with Ellison in more of a “getting to know you” setting. Beyond that, she expressed her desire to stick with the company post-merger: “I love my team at Warner Bros. Television Group. I love our shows, our talent. And I’ve become very happy in my U.S. networks role, which was something that I didn’t see coming almost two years ago. The best-case scenario for me is something that allows me to continue to play around in both of these spaces.”

	Among the possible setups that observers have spitballed was the idea of splitting their oversight between networks and studios. But if Cheeks does take control of the entire TV business, the biggest question will be whether Dungey will opt to remain and report to him. Insiders say the two have a good rapport, particularly as Warner Bros. TV has been a hefty supplier of series to CBS over the years — including the successful crop of Chuck Lorre comedies that have aired on the Eye.

	Beyond that, the question also remains as to how Warner Bros. TV (run by president Brett Paul and creative affairs president Clancy Collins White), CBS Studios (run by president David Stapf), and Paramount TV Studios (run by Matt Thunell) will all be integrated. 
	

	CBS Studios is also a major enterprise, producing more than 60 series, while Paramount TV Studios has a hefty slate including the Taylor Sheridan shows. 

	Currently, Stapf and Thunell report to Cheeks, while Paul and Collins White report to Dungey. There could be a scenario where Warner Bros. TV, CBS Studios and Paramount TV Studios continue as separate labels.

	Cheeks had previously been president and CEO of CBS, having joined Paramount in March 2020. This repped his second stint there, having first joined MTV Networks (a part of the then-Viacom company) in 1998 and later taking on roles including exec VP of business affairs and general counsel for the Viacom Music and Entertainment Groups.

	Cheeks later moved to NBC in 2012 as president of business operations and late-night programming, then became co-chairman of NBC Entertainment and later as vice chairman of NBCUniversal Content Studios. 

	Deadline was first to report of Cheeks’ potential new role at Skydance.

schema.headline: George Cheeks May Be Poised for Expanded TV Role at Skydance Post Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger

title: Skydance Shuffle: David Ellison Addresses Troops About New Name, Says Adieu to Mike and Pam and Sets Table for ‘Barbie 2’
description: It’s 102 degrees in Los Angeles, but it’s certainly not a summer Friday on the Paramount lot. The studio is swarming with activity, subplots and pre
body:
It’s 102 degrees in Los Angeles, but it’s certainly not a summer Friday on the Paramount lot. The studio is swarming with activity, subplots and preparations for the closing of Skydance‘s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery next week.The industry is obsessively speculating on who survives the merger to be named to David Ellison‘s executive leadership team come Monday. But first thing’s first — Ellison addressed his troops on the combined company’s new name. It’s Skydance, same as the company Ellison founded 20 years ago, and will be the parent to existing brands like Warner Bros., Paramount and HBO.“As we bring Paramount and Warner Bros. together, we wanted to preserve what has made each of these studios iconic. Both have distinct identities, extraordinary legacies and brands that have resonated with audiences for generations,” Ellison wrote to staff in a memo obtained by Variety. “We never wanted a new corporate identity to diminish, alter or overshadow either one. Instead, we wanted a name that would give the combined company an identity of its own while allowing Paramount and Warner Bros. — and all our extraordinary brands — to remain in the spotlight.”Remain they will, though under various layers of oversight. Paramount Pictures leaders Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein will be elevated to an expansive creative post, multiple sources tell Variety, overseeing heads of individual film labels across both companies (like New Line stalwart Richard Brener). With this week’s exit of Paramount+ streaming head Cindy Holland, Casey Bloys is the presumptive ruler of all streaming at Skydance. The company has yet to make anything official.Variety confirmed late Thursday night that Warner Bros. Motion Picture Group heads Pamela Abdy and Michael De Luca are out. The decision shocked them, insiders said, though another power player with knowledge of the duo remarked that if they were surprised, “they’re the only ones.” Their fate has been one of the biggest question marks looming over the entire deal. Timing wasn’t on their side, as the motion picture group stacked dizzying losses for WBD this year (despite a banner 2025). Another source added that Ellison personally spoke to the pair on Friday. Today is thought to be their last day on the Warner Bros. lot in Burbank.While Ellison won’t get the keys to WBD until next week’s formal close, dealmaking activity is surging. Goldberg and Greenstein have been reaching out to key talent at Warner Bros. (like Margot Robbie and her LuckyChap partners) to establish continuity. Another knowledgeable source said that wheels are already turning to lock in a sequel to Greta Gerwig‘s “Barbie,” which we previously reported had flatlined over costs. Keep in mind, Ellison just tapped former Mattel CEO Ynon Kriez to be the co-CEO at the new combined company.

	“There’s no way ‘Barbie 2’ doesn’t happen,” said the source.
	
	Team,I am excited to share the new name of our combined company, Skydance.We chose this name for a few important reasons. First and foremost, as we bring Paramount and Warner Bros. together, we wanted to preserve what has made each of these studios iconic. Both have distinct identities, extraordinary legacies and brands that have resonated with audiences for generations. We never wanted a new corporate identity to diminish, alter or overshadow either one. Instead, we wanted a name that would give the combined company an identity of its own while allowing Paramount and Warner Bros. — and all our extraordinary brands — to remain in the spotlight.Of course, Skydance also carries deep meaning for me. I chose the name for my own studio 20 years ago because I wanted something truly personal that also represented limitless possibility. The personal part came from my love of flight: skydancing is another name for aerobatic flying. The possibility came from the cosmos, which to me represents boundless potential and the large-canvas storytelling of cinema. Even our original logo reflected that idea, with each letter of Skydance representing a planet revolving around the sun. From the beginning, the name was meant to capture what great storytelling can do: transport people to places they might never otherwise go and take us beyond the limits of the world we know — and even our own imaginations. That sense of scale, discovery and ambition feels especially fitting for what we are building today.We have big goals for Skydance, and we intend to pursue them with passion, imagination and a willingness to take smart risks. At the same time, we will honor what makes Paramount and Warner Bros. special — giving both studios the opportunity to grow, tell more great stories and bring those stories to even broader audiences around the world, powered by the scale and capabilities of Skydance.Welcome to Skydance. I couldn’t be more excited about what we’re going to build together.David

schema.headline: Skydance Shuffle: David Ellison Addresses Troops About New Name, Says Adieu to Mike and Pam and Sets Table for ‘Barbie 2’

title: ‘Digger’: How Its Big Twist Saves the Movie From Being a Complete Disaster (Opinion)
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains major spoilers for “Digger,” in theaters now via Warner Bros.

	When does a bad movie become a fascinating watch?
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains major spoilers for “Digger,” in theaters now via Warner Bros.

	When does a bad movie become a fascinating watch?

	So often the kiss of death for a feature is boredom; that feeling you’ve seen the same story many times before, the actors are checked out, there’s no visual panache. That’s not the case with “Digger.” While it’s shaping up to be a box office disaster, the movie is anything but dull. Tom Cruise leads the cast in acting to the rafters, DP Emmanuel Lubezki keeps the camera moving and director Alejandro G. Iñárritu injects plenty of swagger in the proceedings.
	

	Unfortunately, the film’s opening — an extended introduction to Cruise’s ambitious oilman Digger Rockwell — is so in-your-face that it sags under the weight. Cruise is in grotesque prosthetics, eager to show us as quickly as possible how uncouth Digger is: He eats from the same can of sardines as his beloved cat, his butt crack is seen in plain view of his maid, his comb-over wisps wildly.


	It’s a clichéd character surrounded by other bobbling caricatures that enter and exit the rooms of his mansion, flailing wildly as Digger learns that his oil company might have inadvertently caused a climate-based global disaster. It’s shrill and tired, and despite the best intentions of the filmmakers to cause provocation around environmentalism, it’s about as subtle as Cruise turning to the camera and screaming, “DO YOU GET IT?!?” Ultimately, the poster’s promise of “a comedy of catastrophic proportions” seems more like a threat than a guarantee of “Dr. Strangelove”-esque genius.
	

	But then, an interesting twist happens. No, “Digger” isn’t a musical, but rather reveals that everything we’ve seen so far is a group of actors rehearsing an ambitious play about Digger called “Fossil Fools.” We’re witnessing the tech rehearsal hours before the show is set to debut in front of an audience, and Cruise drops his broad southern accent, revealing himself as Curtis Markson, the star of the show who has difficulty finding the satirical rhythm.

	It’s an engagingly meta turn, and shows much more of Cruise’s psyche than audiences might expect. During a teflon press tour hyping “Digger,” journalists weren’t able to conjure anything personal or interesting from him. But during a scene where Cruise argues with “Fossil Fools” director Hannah (Sophie Wilde) about satire versus real-world events, the artifice of Cruise’s fat suit and cowboy boots melts away, and the fire in his eyes that made iconic performances in films like “Magnolia” and “Eyes Wide Shut” blaze returns in flashes.

	It also helps to contextualize Iñárritu’s vision of satire itself. Some reviews of “Digger” have knocked the very idea of satirical films in 2026. After all, how can anything feel larger-than-life in the Trump era? But given the put-on-a-show staging, the film’s structure adds further firepower to standout scenes like Digger holding court in the United Nations, tap-dancing around a global community ready to feed him to the wolves after he doubles down on his wrongdoing.

	The showcase scene is emphasized by the fact that everything is underwritten by Digger’s real-life nephew Kenny (Jesse Plemons), who bought the rights to “Fossil Fools” and used his vast wealth to fund the production. His motivations are many, as he implies that he’s doing it out of a mix of penance, flagellation and tribute to his family name. But ultimately he’s a benefactor of the arts. The themes make it impossible to ignore the real-life soap opera currently happening at “Digger” studio Warner Bros., where new owner David Ellison swears he bought the company for all the right reasons.

	“Digger” ends on a somber note, with the audience methodically putting on gas masks and emptying the gorgeous theater, stepping into the dystopian world that remains after Digger’s environmental disaster. Flooded streets, discarded cars and military police are all around, until the camera tilts to the sky and the soundtrack becomes overwhelmed with the natural noises of wild animals. It’s a chilling wrap, as well as a dour end to what appears to be the last Warner Bros. film ever released.
	

	Not all of the elements tied to the twist work — Curtis’ search for his daughter’s missing flight during the tech rehearsal is curiously underbaked — but at least it teases a flurry of ideas instead of drowning in clumsy dialogue. At its best, it recalls Charlie Kaufman’s far superior 2008 film “Synecdoche, New York,” in which Philip Seymour Hoffman is a theater director who, in the pursuit of truth, creates a full-scale recreation of New York City in a warehouse in order to accurately reflect life. It, too, looks at the idea of understanding larger truths through a stage production, but is more clever and sincere.

	Ultimately, even the decision to add another layer, becoming a story about art just as much as one about the climate crisis, doesn’t escalate “Digger” into must-see territory. But the cross section of cinephiles who will be compelled to catch it in theaters — Cruise completists, flop aficionados, rubberneckers who want to see the world burn — will have more to chew on than the artifice presented at the beginning.

schema.headline: ‘Digger’: How Its Big Twist Saves the Movie From Being a Complete Disaster (Opinion)

title: ‘Behemoth!’ Review: Pedro Pascal Is a Classical Cellist Skating Through a Midlife Crisis in Tony Gilroy’s Elevated Bauble of a Music Drama
description: I was a classical musician growing up, so I’m probably more disposed than most to like a movie set in the classical-music world. Then again, that co
body:
I was a classical musician growing up, so I’m probably more disposed than most to like a movie set in the classical-music world. Then again, that could mean that I set a higher bar for authenticity when it comes to depicting it. There’s no doubt that the cinema’s reigning masterpiece of classical-music drama is “Tár” — a great movie in so many other ways that that remains only one dimension of it. But Todd Field inhabited that world, and allowed the audience to do so, in a way that no previous director had. Two other films leap to mind that have the ring of deep-dish classical-music reality: “Mr. Holland’s Opus,” which beautifully caught the experience of studying music in high school, and “Maestro,” a movie I may have enjoyed more than others, even though it left out a ton of stuff about Leonard Bernstein (like, for instance, the heart of his conducting career in the ’50s and ’60s!), because I instinctively filled all of that in.
	

	Viewed on that scale, “Behemoth!,” Tony Gilroy’s drama about a professional cellist, played with perky mystery by Pedro Pascal, scores on the level of authenticity. Pascal’s character, a renowned musician named Alex Serian, has been a member of various world-class symphony orchestras, notably in Chicago, but the film presents us with a more plugged-in contempo angle on this kind of career. In the new era, orchestras are foundering, the pay isn’t what it used to be, and even a virtuoso string musician might need a side gig or two. For Alex, that has meant playing in orchestras that are assembled to record movie scores — a major industry, and one that “Behemoth!” depicts as being nearly as high maintenance as the prestige symphony circuit.
	

	The conductors who oversee the recording of the movie scores are portrayed as hyper-demanding corporate perfectionists. (One of them, a prima donna played by Thomas Kretschmann, makes it feel like you’re seeing Klaus Kinski going to work for Skydance.) And from the film’s opening scene, which immerses us in the lingo of rehearsal, which is a mixture of old-school classical Euro directives (“pianissimo”) and Hollywood jargon (“new ink”), we’re right there in the cavernous recording studio, feeling the heat and the nuance.

	My all-time pet peeve in classical-music films is that characters who are supposed to be playing the violin or cello almost never look real — you can see from a mile away that they’re faking it, imitating the finger and bow movements like crude mimes. Tony Gilroy has solved this problem in the most committed way possible: He had Pedro Pascal learn to play the cello. That’s really Pascal doing it, which is why everything about his motions looks real, from the vibrato to the bowing to the way he moves his head. That devotion works for the film. It allows us to feel that Alex is as genuine in his talent as a professional athlete or a star chef. Virtuosity is the air he breathes. Not every orchestra player is a virtuoso, of course, but Alex, we learn, was a child prodigy who came from a high-powered musical family (we see a clip of him playing Bach as a 6-year-old on “The Tonight Show”). That’s his pedigree, and it’s also his problem, since the family craziness has messed him up.

	In addition to presenting its musical demimonde with reverent accuracy, “Behemoth!” has another quality going for it: The film is playful. It’s not a symphony — it’s a scherzo. This is only the fourth feature Gilroy has directed (it’s his first since “The Bourne Legacy” in 2012), but coming off the “Star Wars” television series “Andor,” which he created and was the showrunner for, he makes his enthusiasm for the filmmaking process palpable. For most of the film, Alex is doing movie-score session work, and Gilroy introduces an impish device: We see and hear the orchestra recording a score (the music might be suspenseful, romantic, pensive), until seconds later it becomes the score of “Behemoth!” itself. I’m not honestly sure I can say what this slightly meta gambit accomplishes, but it’s clever and fun. Gilroy got no less than nine acclaimed film composers to contribute their talents to the movie (they include James Newton Howard and Alan Silvestri and are billed as the Behemoth! Collective). But he could easily have executed the exact same trick with just one composer.
	

	Leaping around in time, Gilroy draws us into Alex’s world with an effervescent wink at the badness of his behavior. Alex is wriggling out of a fling with Carol, the wife of one of the Chicago orchestra’s wealthy patrons — she’s played by Olivia Wilde, who radiates such intense stalker energy here that we’re not quite sure how to react. Alex just keeps calm, and that’s what Pascal does, more or less, throughout the movie. Alex’s life is falling apart, yet somehow he’s the eye of the storm; everyone around him is screwier than he is. With an elegant mustache and perfect gelled hair that dips down onto his forehead, Pedro Pascal has never looked more dashing — he’s like a refined Burt Reynolds, or maybe a passive Brando. Between his classical chops and his glamorous looks, women drop for Alex, but he’s an artist who has drifted through life, drinking and having flings, always ready to move on to the next woman and the next city and the next gig. It’s a frictionless life he revels in. But something’s got to give.

	Gilroy seems to have been influenced by the elliptical quality of “Tár,” though not always to good effect. I enjoyed, to a point, the cut-and-paste chronology of “Behemoth!,” but there’s a flaw in it: The actors look identical in every scene, so some of it is confusing — like the episode in Dallas where Alex meets Nadia (Eva Victor), a star violinist who seems his match. They sleep together. But then, after a fraught phone conversation with the billionaire who wants to marry her, she lashes out at Alex (who has done nothing wrong), and we’re not sure where this is going or why. A few scenes later, tragedy has struck. But did all these events happen one after another or years apart? We figure it out, but Gilroy should have made it easier to read.

	Alex, after the debacle of his break-up with Wilde’s clingy diva in Chicago, returns to Los Angeles, where he grew up. He can get session work there, and does. He still seems mellow, but he’s bestirred by a pet obsession: listening to the original avant-pop compositions posted online by Viviana (Alexa Swinton), a 15-year-old girl who has become a local celebrity. It turns out that he’s got a connection to her; she’s Nadia’s daughter. But why is he so interested? He’s just got…a feeling.
	

	Alex’s brother, a talented but scruffy podcast host, is played by Will Arnett with a lived-in self-doubt more interesting than anything about his character in “Is This Thing On?” It’s through their conversations that we start to piece together Alex’s troubled family life — but here, once again, Pascal suffers in such a placid way that we keep wanting more. The movie finally comes to a head in an expertly staged suspense sequence where Alex, pretending to be a caterer’s assistant, sneaks into Nadia’s stone mansion, finds what he was looking for, and then has to sneak out. Naturally, the music playing under all this is “movie music.”

	What, in the end, is “Behemoth!,” apart from a movie with a dismally bad title? (You can’t remember it. You can’t pronounce it. And it’s hard to say what, exactly, it means or why it carries an exclamation point — though it is, of course, the title of one of the films that Alex is helping to record the score for.) “Behemoth!” is a midlife-crisis movie. It’s a classical-musician movie. It’s a mild romantic mystery. It’s Tony Gilroy fiddling around with pure movie form. (He’s a sly orchestrator of big-screen storytelling.) But 19 years after “Michael Clayton,” he’s still looking for a subject that will allow him to do what he did so masterfully in that movie: heighten our perceptions of the world along with our emotions, until they become one.

schema.headline: ‘Behemoth!’ Review: Pedro Pascal Is a Classical Cellist Skating Through a Midlife Crisis in Tony Gilroy’s Elevated Bauble of a Music Drama

title: John Leguizamo Has a Message for David Ellison: ‘Think of What Americans Need and What the Industry Needs’
description: John Leguizamo is speaking out about the Paramount and Warner Bros. merger, and he’s imploring David Ellison to consider what the industry needs as
body:
John Leguizamo is speaking out about the Paramount and Warner Bros. merger, and he’s imploring David Ellison to consider what the industry needs as he takes over the new Skydance. 

	“Come on, Dave. Do the right thing. Don’t just think of yourself and your pocket. Think of what Americans need and what the industry needs. Think of others for a change.”

John Leguizamo has a message for Skydance chief David Ellison:“C’mon, Dave. Do the right thing. Don’t just think of yourself and your pocket. Think of what Americans and the industry needs. Think of others for a change.” pic.twitter.com/DjEUzXvWja— Variety (@Variety) October 2, 2026


	Although the terms of the merger include Paramount-WBD being prohibited from selling the Paramount Studios or Warner Bros. lots in California for at least five years. Leguizamo said “that’s still not enough.”
	

	“You got an end date. You got an expiration date. That’s not cool,” he said. “People have to plan for the rest of their lives. They plan for five years, and then what?”


	“…The industry belongs in L.A.,” Leguizamo said Friday at the Critics Choice Association’s 6th Annual Celebración of Cinema & Television, where he was honored with the Career Achievement Award. “We need to support it and grow it. Rebuild it and add to it. Not subtract.”

John Leguizamo says it’s “despicable” and “heartless” that David Ellison’s Skydance is threatening to move Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery’s film and TV production out of Los Angeles.When Variety’s @marcmalkin brought up the five-year production commitment in Ellison’s… pic.twitter.com/yj2YwtwAcG— Variety (@Variety) October 2, 2026


	In April, Leguizamo was one of more than 4,000 film and TV stars and creatives who signed an open letter opposing Paramount Skydance’s pending acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.

	“We are deeply concerned by indications of support for this merger that prioritize the interests of a small group of powerful stakeholders over the broader public good,” said the letter, which was published by the New York Times and available on the website BlocktheMerger.com. “The integrity, independence, and diversity of our industry would be grievously compromised. Competition is essential for a healthy economy and a healthy democracy. So is thoughtful regulation and enforcement.”
	

	Other signatories included Joaquin Phoenix, Ben Stiller, Kristen Stewart, Robert De Niro, Sofia Coppola, Florence Pugh, Pedro Pascal, Edward Norton, Atsuko Okatsuka, Adam McKay, Alan Cumming, Alyssa Milano, Boots Riley, Bryan Cranston, Cynthia Nixon, Damon Lindelof, David Fincher, Denis Villeneuve, Elliot Page, Glenn Close, Jane Fonda, JJ Abrams, Jason Bateman, John Leguizamo, Lin-Manuel Miranda, Margaret Cho, Mark Ruffalo, Noah Wyle, Patti Lupone, Ramy Youssef, Rosario Dawson, Rosie O’Donnell, Ted Danson, Tiffany Haddish, Tig Notaro, Yorgos Lanthimos and Yvette Nicole Brown.

	Leguizamo also talked about receiving the Career Achievement Award. “It means they five that to you when you think your career is over,” he cracked, before continuing, “I’ve been in it for four decades, a long time, a lot of sacrifices, a lot of great things, a lot of pain and it feels like, ‘Oh, wow. It was worth for something. People notice and recognize what you’ve done and contributed to cinema.’”

John Leguizamo calls “Mission: Impossible — Reckoning” a “bomb so expensive they teach it in business school.”via The Critics Choice Association's 6th Annual Celebración Of Cinema & Television pic.twitter.com/Z7NLXqG8sW— Variety (@Variety) October 2, 2026


	He delivered emotional remarks while accepting the award from director Gregory Nava. “I will not be finished until every Latin child in this country can turn on a screen,” he said, tearing up. “When a Latin child in this country can turn on a screen and see their own face, their own name, their grandma’s accent, not getting arrested, not dying in minute nine [of an action movie], just living, just being a whole person, that’s the dream. It’s an embarrassingly small one, but they’ve made us fight over it for over a hundred years. So keep creating. Keep failing forward and don’t’ let anyone every quiet your voice, including the one inside your head telling you that you’re not good enough. That voice is a fucking liar and it doesn’t know what the hell it’s talking about.”

	Honorees also included Aimee Carrero (Supporting Actress Award – Series; “Your Friends & Neighbors”), Beth de Araújo (Breakthrough Director Award; “Josephine”), Inde Navarrette (Breakthrough Actress Award – Film; “Obsession”), James Ortiz (Innovator Award; “Project Hail Mary”), Javier Calvo & Javier Ambrossi, popularly known as “Los Javis” (Director Award; “La Bola Negra”), Judy Reyes (Trailblazer Award; “High Potential”), Laysla De Oliveira (Breakthrough Actress Award – Series; “Lioness”), Oscar Nuñez (Vanguard Award; “The Paper”), Peter Dager (Rising Star Award; “Stick”) and Rodrigo Teixeira (Producer Award; “Paper Tiger”).

schema.headline: John Leguizamo Has a Message for David Ellison: ‘Think of What Americans Need and What the Industry Needs’

title: Projeto Paradiso Founder Olga Rabinovich to Receive Inaugural Encounters Award at the São Paulo Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Philanthropist Olga Rabinovich will receive the inaugural Prêmio Encontros (Encounters Award) at this year’s Encontro de Ideias Audiovisuais, the in
body:
Philanthropist Olga Rabinovich will receive the inaugural Prêmio Encontros (Encounters Award) at this year’s Encontro de Ideias Audiovisuais, the industry platform of the São Paulo International Film Festival. The award honors her enduring commitment to advancing Brazilian cinema and elevating the international profile of Brazilian film and talent through her work with Projeto Paradiso.

	The Encounters Award was created to spotlight the transformative role of private investment in culture, bringing together private funders and the creative professionals behind audiovisual productions. The inaugural honor will be bestowed upon Rabinovich during the event’s opening gala ceremony on Oct. 14 and ahead of an in-conversation event with Neon president Jeff Deutchman.
	

	Born in São Paulo, Rabinovich spent years volunteering in hospitals, working closely with terminally ill patients. In 2018, she founded the Olga Rabinovich Institute, launching Projeto Paradiso soon after. The initiative is dedicated to the advancement of the Brazilian audiovisual sector and grew out of her belief that “stories can change the world,” as well as a decision to invest in the people who create them and want to share them with audiences worldwide.


	“Olga Rabinovich is the first recipient of the newly created Prêmio Encontros, because she was the inspiration behind the award,” said Renata de Almeida, director of the São Paulo International Film Festival. I first heard Olga’s name in early 2018, when Josephine Bourgois came to see me about someone from the private sector who wanted to create an institute dedicated to cinema. The Olga Rabinovich Institute was announced during the 42nd Mostra, bringing a breath of hope at a time that promised to be particularly difficult for Brazilian film and culture.”
	

	“Eight years later, Projeto Paradiso, an initiative of the Olga Rabinovich Institute, has already made a major contribution to discovering and championing a new generation of talent, strengthening Brazil’s audiovisual sector as a whole,” continued the director. “Projeto Paradiso has an outstanding professional team, as its results clearly demonstrate. But the image that stays with me is of a meeting with Olga, climbing the winding stairs of our little building for a somewhat chaotic coffee in the festival’s office. Because, in the end, almost everything really does begin with an encounter.”



	

					Courtesy of Milena Palladino
	



	Earlier this year, Variety sat down with the philanthropist ahead of the third Projeto Paradiso National Network Meeting in Brazil’s buzzy production hub of Recife. Rabinovich said she “loved the idea of supporting cinema because I feel it is a magical art form.” “You enter a screening room without knowing whether you’ll be elated or disturbed or moved. It’s a transformative experience. I think it’s incredible to have a communal artistic experience that moves you like this.”

	Projeto Paradiso offers a wide range of support to Brazilian screen professionals to maximize their presence on the global stage, supporting the development of stories through fellowships, residencies, workshops, and other training and international reach initiatives. The Paradiso Talent Network now comprises 278 Brazilian professionals. 

	The organization also helps connect Brazilian talent and projects with the international industry through a network of more than 250 partner institutions in Brazil and abroad, including the Hubert Bals Fund, La Fabrique Cinéma de l’Institut français, TorinoFilmLab, Film Independent and the Sundance Institute.

	The initiative was recently behind buzzy festival titles such as Allan Deberton’s Berlinale-winning “Gugu’s World” and Grace Passô’s “Our Secret,” and boasts a talent network of 264 professionals, including Anita Rocha da Silveira (“Medusa”), Juliana Rojas (“Good Manners”) and Dira Paes (“Manas”).

	In 2025 Projeto Paradiso teamed with the Embratur Brazilian Tourism Board to launch Screen Brasil, offering four Brazilian films a year in two calls – the latest of which closed Oct. 2 supporting their international distribution campaigns, submissions being made by the international sales agent holding the film’s commercial rights. Announced at Cannes Marché du Film this May, films backed to date take in Gabriel Mascaro’s “The Blue Trail,” Rafaela Camelo’s “The Nature of Invisible Things” and animated feature “Papaya.”
	

	Projeto Paradiso’s relationship with the São Paulo International Film Festival dates back to 2018, when the philanthropy initiatve was launched during the festival’s 42nd edition. Since then, Projeto Paradiso has steadily expanded its presence at the festival. 

	Since 2023, it has presented the annual Paradiso Distribution Support Award, providing a distribution grant for the theatrical release of a fiction feature. In 2024, Projeto Paradiso was also one of the driving forces behind a new partnership with the Hubert Bals Fund (HBF), which led to the creation of HBF+Brazil following initial discussions at Encontro de Ideias.

	The 50th edition of the São Paulo International Film Festival runs Oct. 15-29.

schema.headline: Projeto Paradiso Founder Olga Rabinovich to Receive Inaugural Encounters Award at the São Paulo Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Skydance Blasts Off: Can David Ellison Make Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Fly?
description: David Ellison has emerged victorious. And he’s boldly — or arrogantly, if you prefer — decided to name the entertainment giant that he’s bolted toge
body:
David Ellison has emerged victorious. And he’s boldly — or arrogantly, if you prefer — decided to name the entertainment giant that he’s bolted together Skydance Corp., nodding to the original name of his film production firm that has swallowed up two Hollywood studios over the past 14 months.

	Defying skeptics and beating back opponents, Ellison has harpooned his white whale in buying Warner Bros. Discovery. Now he has to prove that the $111 billion mega-merger can become a profitable entertainment powerhouse, and not just a vessel that will get sucked under by a massive whirlpool of debt.
	

	As the closing of the deal — set to occur Tuesday, Oct. 6 — became a certainty, entertainment industry insiders started to come to grips with the reality that the enlarged company is a new and unpredictable force in town. The deal has been polarizing for the creative community, with many boldface names going public in their opposition to the merger. The new leadership team that Skydance is assembling under the direction of Ellison and Ynon Kreiz, just recruited from Mattel to serve as co-CEO, has to navigate that dynamic. And they must do it while walking a tightrope on Wall Street to pay down debt and grow profits across film, linear TV and streaming.


	“They need to move as quickly as possible to get the leverage down,” says Jawad Hussain, managing director at S&P Global. “The biggest hurdle and the biggest thing we’re going to be keeping our eye on is integration and execution.” Two years ago, Hussain says, Skydance Meida was a small company that turned out a few films a year. “Now it’s managing one of the largest media companies. It’s not necessarily an easy task.”
	

	It’s all been a whirlwind. On the morning of Sept. 30, Ellison still didn’t know if it was a done deal.

	He had spent more than a year in his relentless pursuit of acquiring Warner Bros. and HBO. The WBD board rejected his takeover offers eight times. David Zaslav, Warner Bros. Discovery’s boss, ghosted Ellison in December 2025 after Netflix clinched a deal for WB’s streaming and studios business. But Ellison didn’t surrender; he finally outbid Netflix in February, with a $31/share offer that was nearly 2.5 times the stock price before the M&A frenzy kicked off. It was an offer WBD couldn’t refuse.

	Ellison and his legal team, headed by former DOJ official Makan Delrahim, predicted the proposed Paramount-WB combo would easily clear regulatory approvals. In June, Trump’s Justice Department rubber-stamped the pact without attaching any conditions. All told, regulators in 68 jurisdictions worldwide cleared the merger with minimal pushback.

	The last barricade in Ellison’s way? An antitrust lawsuit brought by 12 Democratic state attorneys general, led by California’s Rob Bonta. Ellison believed the litigation was politically motivated, stoked by fears he would try to turn CNN into a Trump-friendly mouthpiece. (He has repeatedly promised a hands-off approach to CNN’s news coverage.) But the AGs pressed their case and a federal judge agreed that their arguments — that Paramount-Warner Bros. would wield undue power in theatrical and basic cable markets — had merit. A trial was scheduled to begin in March 2027.

	Frustrated and incredulous, Ellison let it be known through press leaks in August that he would pull Paramount out of California if the state AGs didn’t let him close the WB deal. Paramount insiders continue to insist the notion of Ellison’s Golden State exit wasn’t a bluff or a threat. Bonta, seeming to realize he would gain no political capital by derailing or delaying the merger, relented. Paramount and the AGs announced a settlement of the suit on Sept. 21 — with a list of concessions so lenient that it surprised not only industry watchers but also employees at both companies.

	Now all that was left was the judge’s approval of the settlement. Worryingly for Ellison, U.S. District Court Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguin at a Sept. 24 hearing had left the door open to a potential further third-party review of the settlement at the behest of Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.). The groups behind the #BlockTheMerger coalition, which had amassed more than 5,700 signatories from actors, filmmakers and industry workers opposed to the deal, filed a brief with the court urging Martínez-Olguín to reject the settlement.

	But on Sept. 30 at just after 12:30 p.m pacific time, the judge issued her ruling: She had approved the settlement.

	The proposed consent decree, Martínez-Olguin wrote, reflects a “compromise that may leave some dissatisfaction for both sides and the public but a compromise that saves the risk, time and expense of litigating through trial.”

	Boom! Teams at both companies swung into action to make the final preparations needed to close the deal. That evening, Paramount and WBD confirmed the merger’s expected closing date of Oct. 6, at which point Paramount’s common stock will move from Nasdaq to list on the New York Stock Exchange. The stock symbol will change from “PSKY” to “SKYD,” reflecting the Skydance corporate name.

	Ellison is expected to lead a town hall meeting with employees next Tuesday, and Ellison and Kreiz are scheduled to host a virtual press briefing — along with the new Skydance’s executive leadership — at 7 p.m. ET on Oct. 6.

	Coincidentally, on Sept. 30 Ellison had been sitting on his own bit of hot news: He was ready to announce that he recruited media vet Kreiz to be co-CEO at the combined Paramount-WBD. The merged entity’s businesses will jointly report to Ellison and Kreiz.

	Word of Kreiz’s joining Paramount trickled out earlier in the day, but Ellison had already decided to wait until after market close to announce it. Paramount put the release on the wire at 1:06 p.m., a little over half an hour after the judge OK’d the antitrust settlement.

	Ellison triumphantly sent Paramount employees a companywide email about Kreiz’s hiring, timestamped at 1:18 p.m., praising the exec as a “proven builder and operator.” Kreiz, during his eight years at Mattel, had helped cut costs through layoffs — and oversaw its first theatrical release, 2023 blockbuster “Barbie.” He swung the company to profitability, but revenue has stubbornly stayed flat the last four years.Ellison wrote in his email: “Together we are well positioned to integrate, operationalize and run the businesses as we build one of the most ambitious next-generation media companies in the industry’s history. Kreiz, as part of his compensation package, will receive $31.5 million in fully vested stock as a signing bonus with the merger close.

	Then on Friday, Oct. 2, Ellison shared on X that the new corporation would be … Skydance. His post included a sizzle reel of the combined company’s biggest hits, leading off with a clip from “Titanic” — an inauspicious choice, perhaps, given how that infamous voyage turned out.
	

	“Paramount and Warner Bros. shaped over a century of culture,” Ellison wrote. “By combining them, we aren’t rewriting history — we’re equipping these iconic studios with a more powerful engine. Together, we are Skydance: a creative-first home for bold, quality storytelling.”

	Three years ago, Ellison was primarily known as a rich kid — scion of Oracle billionaire Larry Ellison, one of the world’s richest people — and a semi-successful movie producer, most notably with 2022’s “Top Gun: Maverick,” which turned in a boffo $1.5 billion at the box office. Now, having bagged Warner Bros., he can lay claim to being a titan in the business and no mere nepo baby.

	“Ellison stared down the attorneys general and won. He stared down the unions and won,” says Prof. Erik Gordon of University of Michigan’s Ross School of Business. “You can’t see David Ellison as daddy’s boy anymore. He’s a formidable force in the industry.”

	The Paramount-WBD merger is the biggest M&A deal in Hollywood history. It brings together two of Hollywood’s biggest movie studios, HBO Max and Paramount+ streaming services dand TV brands including CBS, CNN, MTV, TBS, Comedy Central, Food Network and more. The new company’s entertainment franchises span Harry Potter, Lord of the Rings, Game of Thrones and other HBO hits, the DC superhero universe, “Yellowstone,” “Mission: Impossible,” “Top Gun” and the Nickelodeon kids’ empire.

	“We still have work to do before the deal closes, and nothing changes until it does,” Ellison told employees in his memo about Kreiz.

	But even before the deal closed, the company’s new leadership was taking shape. Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy, co-heads of Warner Bros. Motion Picture Group, will leave post-merger, sources told Variety. Paramount film heads Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein are in line to oversee both movie studios.

	With the deal close, Zaslav is expected to depart — with a boatload of money. Zaslav stands to earn at least $550 million in stock and cash once the Paramount-WBD deal closes, including $34.2 million in cash severance payments, per the terms of his “golden parachute” package.

	Skydance’s settlement-related obligations around theatrical film and the operation of its Paramount and Warner Bros. cable channels will undoubtedly have ripple effects in the marketplace that extend well beyond the U.S. Showbiz leaders in Europe have closely watched the transaction at a time when local-language production is at a peak thanks to the influence of Netflix, Amazon and Disney+. HBO has a growing international footprint that will be crucial to Skydance’s future growth.
	

	Pierre-Antoine Capton, chairman of France’s Mediawan, says the broader film and TV business is in line for a bumpy few years amid the shakeout of what he calls “a period of intense consolidation” of media assets. Mediawan bought Peter Chernin’s North Road Company earlier this year. It’s also circling Lionsgate as a potential acquisition.

	“Having spoken with David, I believe his vision is first and foremost an artistic, creative ambition,” Capton says of the Skydance merger. “He wants to build a more powerful group in order to invest in creation. It’s not only about making cuts. I believe in his commitment to cinema and to theatrical releases.” At the same time, “everywhere in the world we’re entering a much more difficult phase, where consolidation will be, in my view, one of the solutions to the economic problems we’re all going to face,” Capton says.

	Ellison and Kreiz will also be under pressure to deliver a clear roadmap for generating bigger profits from its streaming pillars, HBO Max and Paramount+.

	Casey Bloys, head of WBD’s HBO, is poised to assume oversight of the combined Paramount-Warner Bros. streaming business after Cindy Holland announced on Sept. 29 to staffers that she was stepping down from her role running Paramount+ and other direct-to-consumer businesses.

	Holland’s resignation blindsided some senior managers at Paramount, who thought Ellison had hired her for the long haul. “We all thought we had the home-court advantage — that David was bringing all the new people at Paramount to have them be part of Warner Bros.,” a company insider says.

	Paramount+ and HBO Max will together have more than 200 million subscribers. The newly merged Skydance can save money by consolidating its back-end streaming infrastructure. But “you don’t want to immediately combine the two streaming services because people won’t pay the sum of the two subscription prices,” says Prof. Sridhar Tayur of Carnegie Mellon University’s Tepper School of Business. For the foreseeable future, HBO Max and Paramount+ will continue as discrete brands.

	Another area to watch: what Ellison does with CNN, which throws off operating cash that Skydance Corp. will need to bolster its finances. Ellison has held preliminary talks with CNN chief Mark Thompson about staying on after the merger, sources tell Variety. The prospect of Thompson continuing at the helm, at least for now, came as a relief to CNN personnel, who have been worried that Bari Weiss, the “anti-woke” media entrepreneur Ellison put in charge of CBS News, might extend her fiefdom to include the news cabler.

	Under the settlement with the 12-state coalition, the merged Paramount-Warner Bros. will be subject to monitoring by a “news editorial independence board.” The board, which will include representatives from the states, will establish which will establish “guiding editorial and journalism principles” for CNN and CBS News. But critics have dismissed this as a toothless condition. One player displeased with this outcome was Connecticut Attorney General William Tong, who, although he signed off on the settlement, said afterward he had advocated for a full divestiture of CNN and CBS News.
	

	Foes of ParaBros remain hopping mad. Actor Mark Ruffalo, one of the deal’s most strident critics, has vowed to continue the fight. “This merger will stifle creativity, weaken free speech and cost people their jobs — it is a bad deal for this country and should never have been approved,” he said in a social media post Sept. 30.

	Ruffalo’s feud with Paramount got ugly. On Aug. 21, he posted a message warning about the dangers of the Paramount-WB merger and alleged Larry Ellison’s Oracle was complicit in “what we now have come to see as a genocide” by the Israeli government against Palestinians. Paramount responded forcefully. A company rep asserted the “antisemitic tropes” Ruffalo invoked “aren’t just wrong — they’re a bridge too far.” Ruffalo has been set to reprise his role as an FBI agent in a second season of HBO’s “Task” crime drama. It remains to be seen if Ellison will let bygones be bygones.


	Apart from the shouting, the biggest burning questions about the new entity are about its financial condition. 

	How is Paramount buying Warner Bros. Discovery, which has a market cap that’s six times larger? Paramount is issuing billions in debt securities and securing new loans to help foot the bill. Larry Ellison is bankrolling the WBD merger to the tune of $46.7 billion in equity financing. Paramount also lined up about $24 billion in commitments from the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. In April, Paramount said the three Middle Eastern funds will own 38.5% of the combined entity, but that they will have no board seats or governance representation.

	The new company will be controlled by the Ellison family alongside Gerry Cardinale, founder and managing partner of RedBird Capital Partners. Cardinale’s firm is also pitching in equity for the WBD deal, after funding Skydance’s Paramount Global takeover.

	The new company’s net debt is estimated to be more than $80 billion. That staggering amount would translate into annual interest payments topping $6 billion. Add to that the fact that Paramount-WB, under the settlement with the AGs, is obligated to invest at least $300 million more on film production in the U.S. annually (above what the studios combined spent in 2025).

	Paramount execs have told Wall Street they can achieve $6 billion in cost savings through the merger. But not everyone thinks there’s $6 billion in cost savings to be squeezed out without negative consequences. There are obvious areas of overlap in corporate functions like IT, marketing, procurement and legal. But a big risk in executing a media merger of this scale is cutting into bone — resulting in the loss of creative professionals who are essential to the enterprise, says Prof. Tammy Madsen, a professor of management at Santa Clara University’s Leavey School of Business.
	

	“Creativity matters,” Madsen says. “If you are too aggressive in eliminating redundancies in the creative parts of the company, you could kill the value.”

	Ellison, after the final clearance for the merger came through, wasn’t exactly popping the Champagne just yet. But he did, apparently, pop open some breakfast burritos.

	On Oct. 1 — out of nowhere — employees on the Paramount Studios lot in L.A. and at the company’s offices Burbank were welcomed with buffet breakfasts: French toast, pancakes, egg burritos, shakes, berry bowls, chia pudding and more. One insider says it was the first time they had ever seen the company put out that kind of spread.

	Perhaps it was more like a peace offering, coming before the pain of a first wave of layoffs at the new Skydance expected before the end of the year. The merger could result in the loss of some 4,500 film and TV jobs over three years in L.A. alone, according to a report issued by Los Angeles County in August. Insiders believe layoffs will continue with further rounds into 2027.

	There’s no way around the fact that thousands of employees across the former Paramount and WBD are about to get pink-slipped. But Ellison is betting that through the crucible of consolidation, a stronger company will emerge. “We have big goals for Skydance,” he wrote in his post on X about the new name, “and we intend to pursue them with passion, imagination and a willingness to take smart risks.”

	Marc Malkin, Michael Schneider, Cynthia Littleton, Elsa Keslassy, Matt Donnelly, Angelique Jackson, Brian Steinberg and Gene Maddaus contributed to this story.

            Before 2 lethal injections failed to execute her ... Christa Pike refused her last meal and requested the cheesy dish be given to the homeless instead.
      
    
            When Pike was offered the chance to choose a last meal ... she asked that the $20 allocated for the food be used to buy pizza for the homeless ... the New York Times reported.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As you know ... Pike's execution did not go as planned. Despite being administered 2 lethal injections, Pike complained about pain in her arm before becoming unconscious and snoring.
      

            Pike was rushed to a local hospital ... where her lawyers say she's still unconscious and needs a ventilator.
      
    
            Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has since halted the sole remaining execution this year until a third party can figure out what went wrong.
      
    
            Speaking of ... Pike had a blood condition that may have spared her life.
      
    
            Sitting down with Jakson on TMZ's YouTube series, "In The Know" ... Dr. Joel Zivot -- who had examined Pike -- said that because of her thrombocytosis diagnosis, Pike's platelets may have caused a clot that prevented the pentobarbital from spreading and killing her.

            He continues ...             He concluded his apology by saying ... "Again, I'd like to apologize to anyone who was hurt by my words and will continue to always treat people with kindness and respect."

            A child pop star who was a trainee of the Japanese girls’ idol group DIANNA Project has died. She was only 8 years old.
      
    
            Hirata Runa "passed away peacefully" on Sept. 25 ... according to her X account.
      
    
            The DIANNA Project shared in a statement that the up-and-comer died "due to myocarditis resulting from influenza."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The group -- which asked for privacy on behalf of the family -- added ... "We extend our heartfelt thanks to all the fans who supported Runa Hirata and to everyone involved who provided their support."
      

            Following her last performance -- which took place on Sept. 20, according to The Standard -- Runa wrote ... "Thank you for today too, I appreciate it. It was so much fun."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Just 8 days later, her team wrote on her X account ... "To all the fellow idols who were kind to Ruyu during her lifetime, to the fans who supported Ruyu, to everyone at the agency who made Ruyu an idol, and to all the people who were involved with Ruyu, thank you very much."
      
    
            Myocarditis is inflammation of the middle muscular layer of the heart wall, called the myocardium ... according to the American Heart Association.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            She was only 8 years old.
      
    
            RIP
